draft.title: Punctuation for quoting and citing
card: Quotation marks
Quotation marks go around words taken exactly from a source. They show the reader which words are borrowed and which are your own.
Ellipsis
An ellipsis is three dots (...). It shows that some words inside a quotation have been left out.
Square brackets
Square brackets [ ] show that a writer has changed or added a word inside a quotation, such as swapping "he" for [the captain] so the meaning is clear.
Citation
A citation tells the reader where the words came from, such as the author's name and a page number. It lets the reader find the source.
draft.remember: Each mark has a job: borrow, omit, change or credit the source.

a.q: A student writes: The report said the pool "will open ... in spring". What does the ellipsis show?
opts: Some words were left out of the quotation
A word in the quotation was changed
The words came from a different source
The writer is unsure what the report said
a.why: An ellipsis marks words cut from inside a quotation. Square brackets are the mark for a changed word, so the second option mixes up the two jobs.
a.clue: Think about what the three dots stand in for.

b.q: Original: "She ran the whole race." Jai needs to write about the runner as Mia, using her name in the quote. Which version is correct?
opts: "[Mia] ran the whole race" (Chen 12)
"Mia" ran the whole race (Chen 12)
"...Mia ran the whole race" (Chen 12)
"(Mia) ran the whole race" (Chen 12)
b.why: Square brackets show that Jai changed "She" to Mia, and the citation gives the author and page. An ellipsis is wrong because no words were left out. Round brackets are not the mark for changed words.
b.clue: Which mark tells the reader a word was swapped?

a.best: Some words were left out of the quotation

problems.detail: Why (a) says 'the second option mixes up the two jobs', but options are shown in random order. In this order the 'word was changed' option is fourth, so the reference to a position is wrong and confusing. Name the option by its content instead.
